title: Why Does My AC Keep Turning On and Off?
h1: Why Does My AC Keep Turning Off and On?
description: An AC that turns on and off every few minutes is short cycling. Learn the common causes, from thermostats and filters to refrigerant, and what to do about it.
quick_answer: When an AC turns on and off every few minutes, it is short cycling. Common causes are a poorly placed or failing thermostat, a dirty filter, a frozen or dirty coil, low refrigerant, an oversized system, a clogged condensate drain or an electrical fault. Start with the thermostat and filter, then call for service if it continues.
body:
On a hot day, a healthy air conditioner runs for a solid stretch, shuts off once the house reaches the setpoint, and rests until the temperature drifts back up. If yours starts and stops every few minutes, that's called short cycling. It wastes energy, leaves rooms uneven and puts extra wear on the compressor and electrical parts.

What counts as short cycling?

There's no single number, but runs of only a few minutes followed by quick restarts are a red flag, especially on warm afternoons when the house clearly needs more cooling. Other clues include rooms that never feel fully cool, a house that feels damp or sticky, and an outdoor unit that clicks on and off far more often than it used to.

What are the most common causes?

Thermostat problems

The thermostat decides when the system runs, so it's the first thing to check. A thermostat in direct sun, next to a supply register, near a kitchen or on an exterior wall can read the wrong temperature and shut the system off early. Weak batteries, loose wires and incorrect settings on a newer smart thermostat can cause the same thing.

Dirty air filter

A clogged filter cuts airflow across the indoor coil. The coil can get too cold and start to freeze, and some systems shut down on a safety switch when that happens. Replacing a dirty filter is one of the easiest fixes there is.

Frozen or dirty coils

Ice on the indoor coil or refrigerant lines blocks airflow and confuses the system. A dirty outdoor coil does the opposite, trapping heat until pressure gets too high and a safety control stops the compressor. Either way, the system starts and stops instead of running smoothly.

Low refrigerant

A refrigerant leak drops the pressure in the system. Low-pressure safety switches can shut the compressor off, then let it restart once pressure recovers, over and over. Refrigerant leaks need to be found and repaired by a technician.

An oversized system

If the system is too big for the house, it cools the air near the thermostat very quickly, then shuts off before the rest of the home catches up. You'll notice uneven rooms and a clammy feel because the system doesn't run long enough to pull moisture out of the air. If your system has short cycled since the day it was installed, sizing is a likely suspect.

Clogged condensate drain

Your AC removes water from the air and sends it out through a drain line. If that line clogs with algae or debris, a float switch can shut the system off to prevent an overflow. Once the water drains a little, it may start again, then stop again.

Electrical issues

A failing capacitor, worn contactor, loose connection or overheating compressor can all cause stop-and-start behavior. These parts carry high voltage, so testing and replacing them is a job for a technician.

What can you check yourself?

  1. Confirm the thermostat is set to Cool with the fan on Auto, and replace its batteries if it uses them.
  2. Make sure nothing near the thermostat is heating or cooling it, like a lamp, sunny window or supply register blowing on it.
  3. Replace the air filter.
  4. Open all supply registers and make sure return grilles aren't blocked by furniture.
  5. Look at the outdoor unit and clear debris, plants and stored items around it.
  6. Look for ice on the copper lines. If you see any, turn cooling off and let the system thaw before running it again.
  7. Check the condensate drain area for standing water or an overflowing pan.

If those checks don't change anything, it's time for a diagnosis.

Why does short cycling matter?

The compressor uses the most electricity and takes the most strain when it starts. Every extra start adds wear to the compressor, capacitor and contactor, and they push up energy use. Short cycling also means poor humidity control, so the house can feel sticky even when the thermostat says it's cool. Left alone, a problem like a refrigerant leak or a dirty coil can turn into a compressor failure.

How does a technician find the cause?

We start with the thermostat and its wiring, then check airflow, filter and coil condition. We measure refrigerant pressures and temperatures, test the capacitor and contactor, look at the safety switches and clear the condensate drain. If the system looks oversized for the home, we'll tell you and explain the options. Learn more about our air conditioning repair service or use our contact page to set up a visit.

How do you prevent it?

Regular filter changes and a yearly tune-up before summer prevent most of the causes above. A tune-up includes coil cleaning, refrigerant and electrical checks, and drain line cleaning, which are the same items that cause most short cycling.
faqs: Is it normal for my AC to cycle on and off?

Some cycling is normal. The system should run for a solid stretch, shut off when the house reaches the setpoint and restart later. Runs of only a few minutes with quick restarts, especially on hot days, point to a problem.
Can a thermostat cause short cycling?
Yes. A thermostat in direct sun, near a supply register or with weak batteries or loose wiring can shut the system off too early. Moving or replacing the thermostat sometimes solves the issue.
Can short cycling damage my AC?

It can. Frequent starts wear out the compressor, capacitor and contactor and raise energy use. The underlying causes, like low refrigerant or a dirty coil, can also lead to bigger failures if left alone.
Does an oversized AC short cycle?
Often, yes. An oversized system cools the area near the thermostat quickly and shuts off before the rest of the house catches up, which leaves rooms uneven and the air feeling damp.
